claim: The Greek gods have Roman equivalents: Zeus is Jupiter or Jove, Hera is Juno, Athena is Minerva, Poseidon is Neptune, Hermes is Mercury.
Butler's Odyssey names its hero Ulysses, of Ithaca, son of Laertes; Minerva and Jove act in the story.
The Iliad is set at Troy (Ilium) and tells of Achilles, Hector, Agamemnon, Priam and Helen.
The Norse gods include Odin (also Woden), Thor, Loki and Freya, dwelling in Asgard; Valhalla receives the slain.
Noah builds an ark and survives a flood sent by God.
Moses leads Israel out of Egypt and receives the law at Sinai; Jerusalem is the city of David.
Krishna counsels Arjuna on the field of Kurukshetra.
The Dhammapada records the sayings of the Buddha, called Gotama and the Blessed One.
The Kalevala's heroes are Wainamoinen, Ilmarinen and Lemminkainen; Pohyola is the Northland.
Deucalion and Pyrrha survive a flood sent by Zeus; Bulfinch compares it with the Genesis flood.
Arthur holds court and his knights undertake quests.
Frazer compares rites and myths across traditions; comparative religion is a scheme of analysis, not a tradition.
